Chichester's population increased by around 10,300 between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021). This semi-automated article highlights some of the most notable changes among the local population.

The population passed 120,000

Between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021), the population of Chichester increased by 9.0%, from just under 113,800 in 2011 to around 124,100 in 2021.

The population here increased by a greater percentage than the overall population of the South East (7.5%), and by a greater percentage than the overall population of England (up 6.6% since the 2011 Census).

In 2021, Chichester was home to around 1.1 people per football pitch-sized piece of land, compared with 1.0 in 2011. This area was the joint least densely populated local authority area across the South East.

This article generally uses percentages to enable comparisons over time and between areas. The percentage point change is also used to show the difference between the 2011 and 2021 percentages.

Population growth was higher in Chichester than across the South East

An older Chichester

Between the last two censuses, the average (median) age of Chichester increased by two years, from 46 to 48 years of age.

This area had a higher average (median) age than the South East as a whole in 2021 (41 years) and a higher average (median) age than England (40 years).

The median age is the age of the person in the middle of the group, meaning that one half of the group is younger than that person and the other half is older.

The number of people aged 50 to 64 years rose by just over 3,100 (an increase of 13.4%), while the number of residents between 35 and 49 years fell by around 1,900 (8.5% decrease).

The share of residents aged between 50 and 64 years increased by 0.8 percentage points between 2011 and 2021

Changing relationships in Chichester

Chichester saw the South East's joint largest percentage-point rise in the proportion of people aged 16 years and over who had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership (from 9.3% in 2011 to 10.1% in 2021).

Across the South East, the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership increased from 9.1% to 9.3%, while the percentage in nearby Horsham increased from 8.8% to 9.4%.

These figures include same-sex marriages and opposite-sex civil partnerships in 2021, neither of which were legally recognised in England and Wales in 2011. Same-sex marriages have been legally recognised in England and Wales since 2014 and opposite-sex civil partnerships have been recognised since 2019.

The percentage of adults who had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership in Chichester increased by 0.8 percentage points

Rise in private renting

Of Chichester households, 18.1% rented privately in 2021, up from 14.9% in 2011.

In 2021, just over one in seven households (15.1%) lived in socially rented housing, compared with 14.9% in 2011. The percentage of Chichester households that owned their home (outright or with a mortgage or loan) decreased from 67.2% to 65.4%.

The increase in the percentage of privately-rented homes was greater in Chichester (3.2 percentage points) than across the South East (2.9 percentage points, from 16.3% to 19.2%). Across England, the percentage increased by 3.6 percentage points, from 16.8% to 20.5%.

Private renting in Chichester increased by 3.2 percentage points

Unpaid care in Chichester

In 2021, 4.8% of Chichester residents (aged five years and over) reported providing up to 19 hours of unpaid care each week. This figure decreased from 7.9% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

In 2021, 1.5% of residents (aged five years and over) reported providing between 20 and 49 hours of unpaid care each week, compared with 1.1% in 2011. The proportion of Chichester residents (aged five years and over) that provided at least 50 hours of weekly unpaid care increased from 2.0% to 2.2%.

The decrease in the proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care was greater in Chichester (3.1 percentage points) than across the South East (2.8 percentage points, from 7.3% to 4.5%). Across England, the proportion fell by 2.8 percentage points, from 7.2% to 4.4%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and managed their provision of unpaid care, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care in Chichester decreased by 3.1 percentage points

Religion in Chichester

In 2021, 38.7% of Chichester residents reported having "No religion", up from 24.6% in 2011. The rise of 14.1 percentage points was the largest increase of all broad religious groups in Chichester. Because the census question about religious affiliation is voluntary and has varying response rates, caution is needed when comparing figures between different areas or between censuses.

Across the South East, the percentage of residents who described themselves as having "No religion" increased from 27.7% to 40.2%, while across England the percentage increased from 24.8% to 36.7%.

In 2021, 53.1% of people in Chichester described themselves as Christian (down from 66.1%), while 6.2% did not state their religion (down from 7.6% the decade before).

There are many factors that can cause changes to the religious profile of an area, such as a changing age structure or residents relocating for work or education. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses. Religious affiliation is the religion with which someone connects or identifies, rather than their beliefs or religious practice.

Chichester residents' country of birth

In the latest census, around 108,200 Chichester residents said they were born in England. This represented 87.2% of the local population. The figure has risen from around 101,200 in 2011, which at the time represented 88.9% of Chichester's population.

Scotland was the next most represented, with just over 1,700 Chichester residents reporting this country of birth (1.4%). This figure has remained relatively unchanged from 2011.

The number of Chichester residents born in Wales remained close to 1,300 between the last two census (from 1.1% of the local population in 2011 to 1.0% in 2021)

In 2021, 87.2% of Chichester residents reported their country of birth as England

Health in Chichester

In 2021, 52.3% of Chichester residents described their health as "very good", increasing from 50.3% in 2011. Those describing their health as "good" fell from 34.4% to 33.3%. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

The proportion of Chichester residents describing their health as "very bad" remained 0.8%, while those describing their health as "bad" remained 2.9%.

These data reflect people’s own opinions in describing their overall health on a five point scale, from very good to very bad.

Census 2021 was conducted during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and rated their health, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

In 2021, 0.8% of usual residents said their health was very bad in Chichester

National identity in Chichester

In 2021, 5.1% of Chichester residents did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK. This figure increased from 4.1% in 2011.

In 2021, 1.5% of residents identified with a UK and non-UK national identity, compared with 0.7% in 2011. The percentage of residents in Chichester that identified as "British only" increased from 16.7% to 57.9%.

The increase in the percentage of people who did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK was greater across the South East (1.6 percentage points, from 7.1% to 8.7%) than in Chichester (1.0 percentage points). Across England, the percentage increased by 1.7 percentage points, from 8.2% to 10.0%.

In Census 2021, “British” was moved to the top response option and this may have influenced how people described their national identity. For further information, please see our quality report.

The percentage of people who did not identify with at least one UK national identity in Chichester increased by 1.0 percentage points

Family in Chichester

Of Chichester households, 18.0% included a couple but no children in 2021, down from 19.1% in 2011.

In 2021, just under one in six households (16.6%) included a couple with dependent children, compared with 17.5% in 2011. The percentage of single family households including a couple living with only non-dependent children increased from 5.2% to 5.8%.

The decrease in the percentage of households including a couple but no children in Chichester (1.1 percentage points) was similar to the decrease across the South East (1.4 percentage points, from 18.7% to 17.4%). Across England, the percentage fell by 0.9 percentage points, from 17.6% to 16.8%.

The percentage of households including a couple without children in Chichester decreased by 1.1 percentage points

Change in employment

Of Chichester residents aged 16 years and over, 52.2% said they were employed (excluding full-time students) in 2021, down from 54.2% in 2011.

In 2021, around 1 in 50 people (2.0%) said they were unemployed, compared with 2.4% in 2011. The percentage of retired Chichester residents increased from 29.2% to 29.7%.

The decrease in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over (excluding full-time students) who were employed was greater in Chichester (2.0 percentage points) than across the South East (1.3 percentage points, from 59.0% to 57.6%). Across England, the percentage fell by 0.8 percentage points, from 56.5% to 55.7%.

Census 2021 took place during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, a period of rapid and unparalleled change; the national lockdown, associated guidance and furlough measures will have affected the labour market and our ability to measure it.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were employed (excluding full-time students) in Chichester decreased by 2.0 percentage points

More adults worked short hours

In 2021, 14.1% of Chichester residents aged 16 years and over and in employment said they worked 15 hours or less per week. This figure increased from 12.9% in 2011.

In 2021, just over one in eight people (13.1%) said they worked over 49 hours per week, compared with 16.4% in 2011. The percentage of adults in employment working 31 to 48 hours per week increased from 50.7% to 52.2%.

This area had the country's third highest percentage of people aged 16 years and over and in employment who said they usually worked 15 hours or less per week. Across the country, only South Hams (14.5%) and North Norfolk (14.4%) had a higher percentage of people aged 16 years and over and in employment who said they usually worked 15 hours or less per week.

Working hours may have been affected by the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

The percentage of adults who worked 15 hours or less in Chichester increased by 1.2 percentage points

Disability in Chichester

In 2021, 5.4% of Chichester residents were identified as being disabled and limited a lot. This figure decreased from 6.1% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

In 2021, just under 1 in 10 people (9.8%) were identified as being disabled and limited a little, compared with 8.8% in 2011. The proportion of Chichester residents who were not disabled decreased from 85.0% to 84.8%.

The decrease in the proportion of residents who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot was greater across the South East (1.0 percentage points, from 7.2% to 6.2%) than in Chichester (0.7 percentage points). Across England, the proportion fell by 1.6 percentage points, from 9.1% to 7.5%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived their health status and activity limitations, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot in Chichester decreased by 0.7 percentage points

Ethnic groups in Chichester

In 2021, 1.6% of Chichester residents identified their ethnic group within the "Mixed or Multiple" category, up from 1.0% in 2011. The 0.7 percentage-point change was the largest increase among high-level ethnic groups in this area.

Across the South East, the percentage of people from "Mixed or Multiple ethnic groups" increased from 1.9% to 2.8%, while across England the percentage increased from 2.3% to 3.0%.

In 2021, 95.4% of people in Chichester identified their ethnic group within the "White" category (compared with 96.9% in 2011), while 1.7% identified their ethnic group within the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" category (compared with 1.4% the previous decade).

The percentage of people who identified their ethnic group within the "Black, Black British, Black Welsh, Caribbean or African" category increased from 0.5% in 2011 to 0.6% in 2021.

There are many factors that may be contributing to the changing ethnic composition of England and Wales, such as differing patterns of ageing, fertility, mortality, and migration. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses.
